payload.description:
When install finishes in a repository that already excludes the managed core from its linters, I want it to say nothing, so I can stop training a consumer to skim the region where a tracked CI edit is also reported.

Found by the terminal canary, filed there as term-ip2wz and pressed after it shipped twice unchanged. scaffolds.install_notes tests only whether a config file exists, never what it contains, so it advises extend-exclude on a .ruff.toml that has carried exactly that for releases. The canary verified the exclusion is genuinely in force rather than merely present: ruff format --check over the managed core exits 0 on 54 files.

The same block tells a consumer to hand-edit .pre-commit-config.yaml in a run that separately reports it has just rewritten that file.

Severity is low and nothing fails. The reason it is worth fixing is where it sits: the advice is the tail of the install output, and the tail is also where a re-pin of a tracked CI workflow is announced. Unactionable boilerplate beside a real edit teaches a reader to skip both.

Recorded against myself: this was already a requirement on basicly-fmgwtwi, which is still open, and I shipped two releases without meeting it while telling the canary it was on the record. It was on the record and it was not done.
payload.requirements: the check reads the file rather than testing its presence. A false skip is possible if the path is named for some other reason, and that is accepted and stated rather than guarded, because the cost of a missed note is one line a consumer can still read in the documentation.
payload.title: read the file before advising a change it already carries

payload.acceptance_criteria: external-facts says the control is built from a failure that has been seen rather than an assumed one, and says to check the denominator moved; the always-on surfaces stay under their caps and the projection gates pass
payload.description:
When an agent runs a positive control and it returns zero, I want the rule to say what the control must be built from, so I can stop reading a control's own zero as confirmation.

Asked for by the terminal canary as term-2vkce, and the request is well founded: the rule is in managed core they may never edit, they followed both halves of it, and still got a false reading. The wording said run a positive control and that if the control is empty too the zero belongs to the probe. It never said what the control must be built from.

Their case is the evidence. They planted a table they called ragged; it was valid compact style, so it was never a violation, reported zero, and read exactly like a dead probe. Rebuilt from the defect actually observed - padded cells over an unpadded delimiter row - it reported two errors. What rescued the diagnosis was the denominator: 151 files became 152 when the control was added, which proved the file was read and sent them to the table rather than the tooling.

Three of my own false zeros the same day were the environment answering instead of the code. Theirs is the subtler one and the one the rule did not cover.

Carrying it in their overlay was the fallback, and the objection to that is right: two copies of one rule drift, and ours is the copy every other consumer reads.
payload.requirements: the amendment sits in the existing bullet rather than adding one, because the always-on budget is a standing cost on every consumer. The token cost declared on the fragment is updated to what the projection measures rather than left to drift.
payload.title: amend the positive control rule with what a control must be built from

payload.description:
When a patch release changes nothing the tutorial quotes, I want the page to need one edit rather than five, so I can stop paying a ten minute walkthrough for a version string.

Measured across v0.14.0, v0.14.1 and v0.14.2, all cut on 2026-09-18: each required the whole walkthrough re-run - install, scaffold, create, dor, classify, worktree, land, ship, log, status - and every quoted block matched apart from record ids, commit hashes and sub-second timings. Three runs, zero drift found, five strings edited each time.

The five sites are not one kind of thing and the gate cannot tell them apart. Line 7 is the claim, that every command and output was executed on a named version. Lines 36 and 50 are instructions, the uvx line a reader types. Lines 66 and 68 are transcript, what the tool printed.

The page already elides a timestamp on line 68 with its own convention, so eliding the version beside it is consistent rather than new.

payload.text:
[session handover 2026-09-19] Two releases cut and pushed; a fourth install-advice defect is fixed on main and deliberately unreleased.

STATE. main d0146315, clean, nothing unpushed. Tags v0.15.0 and v0.15.1 both pushed. Version on disk 0.15.1. uv run pytest -q -n 4 = 5909 passed 1 xfailed. uv run basicly verify --mode full = PASS.

SHIPPED IN v0.15.0. basicly install wires a post-merge hook that folds the writer shard a merge brought in and commits it with a record id the commit-msg gate accepts (basicly-z9s4iin). It resolves the engine at RUN time, not install time - a basicly on PATH, else the pinned uvx form - because the canary proved it has no basicly on PATH at all, so an install-time absolute path was a certain break rather than a risk. Both arms exercised under env -i. basicly install --dry-run (basicly-jgim0r0). The tutorial no longer costs a re-record per patch (basicly-8y8rxv4). basicly release refuses a stale tutorial transcript in preflight instead of writing everything and meeting the refusal at the commit gate (basicly-oror9os).

SHIPPED IN v0.15.1, both found by the canary within hours of the v0.15.0 tag. The managed-core exclusion advice was fixed into silence in v0.15.0: the check asked whether a config MENTIONS .basicly/core, never whether it EXCLUDES it, and this repo's own .ruff.toml names the path three times in per-file-ignores (basicly-ajqk150). install --dry-run reported the release's own headline feature as broken, because a dry run never syncs the catalog and so ran the vendored kit against the new engine's flags (basicly-v92kmjv); fixing that exposed a second fault under it, the kit computing its own script path even when a host supplies --command.

ON MAIN, UNRELEASED, OWNER'S CALL 2026-09-18. basicly-ap693b0: install advised adding exclude to the .pre-commit-config.yaml it writes itself, whose hooks lint .basicly/core on purpose - no-comments carries pass_filenames true and a files regex matching .py. Followed literally the advice disabled the gates the install had just written. Now silent until the config carries a hook basicly did not write. Held rather than cut because the canary was still on v0.15.0 and a third tag in one day is a version to skip. SHIPS IN THE NEXT CUT - do not let it sit.

OPEN, AND ONLY THE CANARY CAN CLOSE IT. Arm 1, the real fold: terminal-88 carries .basicly/ledger/pending-main.jsonl at 30k, tracked, committed, never folded, hash d3afd42b recorded so the fold can be proven rather than assumed. It is armed but not exercisable - that side pushed, so it has nothing to pull; the fold fires the first time the other machine pushes and this one pulls. Every fold I have measured was on a shard I minted seconds earlier on a throwaway repo. This is the only real-ledger test there is.

ALSO OPEN. basicly-z79v2cf, a clock flake: test_supervise_board.py asserted 0 <= -1.439611 once inside verify --mode full, passed on re-run and 3 of 3 alone; it compares two clocks rather than one monotonic source. The tutorial claim line still forces a full walk on EVERY release including a patch, because docs-claims compares the transcript against the RELEASED version rather than the version it was recorded against - basicly-8y8rxv4 cut the pin cost, not this one, and it is unfiled. CI runs split across two SHAs on both releases: the tag's own commit ran the release job and a later tracker-only commit ran the other three, so 'green on the release commit' is not literally what exists.

METHOD NOTE WORTH KEEPING. Four defects this session were the same shape - a check that answers a question adjacent to the one asked. Mentions-vs-excludes, the dry run previewing an unsynced kit, a grep for a heading rather than for which file it names, a fixture whose directive was deleted while a comment still carried the path. Every one was caught by a row that MUST behave differently, never by the row that confirmed the hope.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. A seat that crashes re-reads what it had not consumed, rather than losing it.
- R2. Nothing an announcement carries is invisible to a reviewer or to the board.
- R3. No daemon, no second store and no network are introduced.
- R4. An announcement that nobody reads is a selection defect that someone can see, not a silent drop.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. Work is never pushed to a seat, because a seat that is not running cannot receive it.
- R2. Two seats never take the same task.
- R3. A seat takes its next task fast enough to stay inside the cache window, or it is released.
- R4. The order tasks are taken in is the order the existing ranked ready set already publishes, so this adds no second scheduler.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. An operator can see inside a running lane without opening a file on the host.
- R2. What the board shows is what the lane actually emitted, never a summary of it.
- R3. Showing a transcript adds no model call and no subprocess to the board, because the board folds files only.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. The answer names the populations that fill a lane's window, with a share for each, not a hypothesis.
- R2. The measurement is repeatable by someone who did not take it.
- R3. The result is allowed to say the gap is irreducible, and that answer closes the spike rather than failing it.

payload.name: requirements

- R2. A validator dispatched on a record with no stated intended use is refused rather than asked to guess.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. No model ever reports its own suitability for a task, because a persuadable scheduler is not a scheduler.
- R2. A match that could not apply an axis says which axis it could not apply, because a silently partial match is worse than none.
- R3. Adding a fifth axis later does not change the three axes that already exist.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:

- R2. Each child states the intended use it is validated against, separately from the criteria it is verified against.
- R3. The set of children covers every `[TARGET]` passage in section 31A and every decision D-45 through D-50, and claims no part the architecture does not specify.
- R4. No child depends on a part of the design the architecture has not decided.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:

- R2. An open record that was written before the change still yields its criteria after it, with no criterion lost.
- R3. A closed record stays readable as evidence, and nothing rewrites a line of the log to achieve that.
- R4. The second store cannot grow back after the switch.

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
- Given a folded field whose value exceeds a declared producer bound then the write is refused at the seam with the field named, rather than stored.
- Given a folded field within the bound then the write is unchanged and the fold derives the same state.
- Given a refusal then it says which field and what the bound is, so the caller can drop what is derivable instead of guessing.
- Given an existing oversized value already in the log then the fold derives the same state as before and nothing rewrites it.
- Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_kit_tracker_events.py -q plus a seam-level test that a 5 MB field value is refused, against a positive control that a small one is accepted

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:

- Given the kind blind default is still reachable then a test states which caller reaches it and why that is safe, or the default is removed.
- Given the provenance test docstring then it names the mechanism that actually protects those keys.
- Given both corrections then the differential still finds no divergence on a ledger it found none on before.
- Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_kit_tracker_provenance.py tests/test_kit_tracker_migrate.py -q plus a differential run over the committed ledger

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:

- R2. The failure rate the health view reports reflects work that was attempted, not a retry storm.
- R3. An operator can tell a record stopped for repeated launch failure from one stopped for any other reason.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. A dispatch never begins billing differently because a host changed a default.
- R2. If a dispatch would bill against an API key rather than the subscription, that is visible before the pass runs, not after the invoice.
- R3. The pin survives a host upgrade without a person remembering to check.

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
- Given a new requirement document then it carries a machine-checkable section set and a record id that resolves in the tracker.
- Given a requirement document whose sections do not conform then a verify check fails and names the missing section.
- Given an author asks for a new requirement then a scaffold command writes the conforming skeleton rather than the author copying an existing file.
- Given every acceptance criterion a requirement carries is closed then a check reports the document as absorbable rather than deleting it.
- Given the folder holds no requirement document then no gate changes behaviour.
- Demonstrated by: uv run basicly verify --mode fast with a deliberately malformed requirement present, showing the check fail and then pass once corrected

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. The failure mode the seat design names is priced, not assumed.
- R2. The measurement uses the host's own reported usage, derived by two paths that share no step.
- R3. The result can say that holding past the window is cheap, and that answer changes the release rule.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. The engine never assumes a cache window a host has not published.
- R2. A host that publishes no window is handled, and the handling is visible rather than silent.
- R3. A window that the vendor changes is corrected in one declaration, not in every call site.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. A second task in a held session costs materially less than the same task in a fresh one, and the saving is measured rather than assumed.
- R2. A session that cannot start its next task inside the host's cache window is ended, because an idle held session is worse than a fresh one.
- R3. A held session is releasable at any moment without losing work, because everything that must survive it is already written.
- R4. A crash of a held session loses no more than a fresh dispatch would.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. A run's recorded cost is the host's own figure, whichever path produced it.
- R2. The runs the engine over-reports are not the runs whose cost matters most, which today they are.
- R3. A future change that removes the de-duplication fails a test rather than shipping silently.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value:
- R1. A record that cannot state its intended use never reaches a lane.
- R2. An author is told which field is missing, not merely that the record is not ready.
- R3. The backlog of records owing a field is visible and falls over time rather than accumulating silently.

## Trigger

When a pass re-enqueues a pending decision item with new numbers, I want the item to keep its decision id and carry the current detail, so I can answer a budget escalation from accurate numbers.

## Context

`decisions.enqueue` is idempotent per `(issue, kind, question)`. When the item is already pending it returns the existing item at src/basicly/decisions.py:100-102 and never rewrites the detail. `PASS_SPEND_QUESTION` in src/basicly/supervise.py is deliberately constant so a repeatedly refusing pass finds the item it already queued, and the numbers live in the detail for exactly that reason. The consequence is that the detail is frozen at first-queue time and every later refusal leaves it untouched.

Measured on basicly-atrqcd 2026-09-01, base 24a0d6f3. `basicly loop decisions basicly-atrqcd` prints for `basicly-atrqcd#3018546b66`:

- `93153836 tokens forecast; 60000000 remaining under the grant; assumed at the unsizeable-lane bound (measured): basicly-jt0dgi, basicly-3iaw0x, basicly-mfavrh, basicly-rv7q88`

Every number and every classification in that line is now wrong. `supervise.admit_pass_spend` over the same four lanes returns `87214845 tokens forecast; 4345392 remaining under the grant; sized:` all four, with `assumed: ()`. Remaining is off by a factor of 13.8, and the line asserts the lanes are unsizeable when their scopes read.

The detail is the only thing a human sees when answering. `PassSpendAdmission.coverage` exists so an operator can see that a number is an assumption before it is the only thing standing between them and the bill; a frozen copy of that sentence defeats it.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decisions.py`
- `tests/test_decisions.py`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.fixed.md`

## Plan

- integrity: L2
- demonstration: `basicly loop decisions basicly-atrqcd` prints the current forecast and remaining budget for basicly-atrqcd#3018546b66

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- WHEN a pending decision item is re-enqueued with a different detail, THE ITEM SHALL keep its decision id and carry the current detail.
- WHEN a pending item is re-enqueued with an unchanged detail, NO further comment or notification SHALL be produced.
- WHEN `basicly loop decisions <id>` prints a pending item, THE DETAIL SHALL be the one from the most recent enqueue.
- WHEN a stale detail is superseded, THE ORIGINAL SHALL remain readable in the append-only log rather than being overwritten in place.

## Trigger

When a skill states a refusal that the code does not enforce, I want a gate to compare the claim against the flag tables, so I can stop a false claim from reaching a dispatched agent.

## The defect

The `work-tracker` skill carried **three** false statements at once (basicly-7wlhlp), each describing a refusal the code does not make. Every gate in the repository was green throughout. Skill prose is projected, linted for format, and checked for drift against its own source — and never checked against the behaviour it describes.

This is the population a green suite protects least: the consumer is a dispatched agent, so a false claim is not confusion, it is a lane that follows a wrong instruction and files no bug about it. One of the three told the reader that every labelling instruction is false, which would make an agent refuse `loop supervise --label`, the multi-lane path.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read `.basicly/core/skills/work-tracker/skill.yaml` before commit fbf844ba.
2. Note the Refuses section claims `update --add-label` raises, `create` without `--json` is refused, and the ready set is the open records.
3. Check each against `src/basicly/owned_write.py`, `src/basicly/tracker_write.py` and `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/differential.py`.
4. Run `uv run basicly verify --mode fast`, `uv run basicly skills-check --all-default-roots` and `uv run basicly catalog lint`.

Observed: all three claims are false, and every gate reports PASS.
Expected: a claim a skill makes about a refusal is checked against the table that implements it.

## The control that would have caught all three

Proposed by the lane that fixed them. `.scripts/docs_claims.py` already carries the mechanism: an `Assertion` that reads a catalog source and fails when it disagrees with an engine symbol. `_skill_work_types` is the working example, and `tests/test_docs_claims.py` has its anchor-vanished test.

Add an assertion that parses the skill's refusal section and fails when it names an `update` flag that `tracker_argv.UPDATE_LABEL_FLAGS` or `tracker_argv.UPDATE_FIELD_FLAGS` actually translates. That binds the prose to the tables whose change made it false, costs nothing per run, and is a deterministic gate rather than a judged one — which the standing constraints prefer.

## The scope question this raises, and does not answer

34 skills ship. This audited one. Whether the other 33 carry the same class of residue is **unmeasured**, and a per-skill hand audit does not scale. The generalisable form is: a skill that states a refusal names the symbol that implements it, and the gate checks the pair. That is a catalog-schema change, and it is larger than this record. Decide the narrow gate first and let its firing history argue for the general one.

## Scope

- `.scripts/docs_claims.py`
- `tests/test_docs_claims.py`

## Trigger

When the harness drives its full loop in a consumer repository, I want no third-party product to sit in the runtime path, so I can upgrade our own state on our own schedule.

## Context

**Corrected 2026-07-30 after the owner sharpened the criterion.** The first version of this epic
read the directive as "zero runtime dependencies" and set out to remove `jinja2`, `jsonschema`,
`pyyaml`, `rich`, `uv`, the pre-commit framework and node. That was wrong, and the correction
matters because it removes a large breaking change from the roadmap.

The axis is not external-versus-internal, nor binary-versus-package. It is:

> **Can we absorb this component's breaking change on our own schedule, or does it dictate terms
> to us?**

A **library or framework** is fine. It is versioned, we pin it, and when it ships a breaking
change we upgrade when ready and fix our own code. The blast radius is our source.

A **product** is not. `beads` is the case in point, and the evidence is already recorded in
`docs/design/work-tracker.md` section 2.10: crossing one of its schema migrations requires
*"exactly one designated clone"* to run `bd migrate` and `bd dolt push` while every other clone
installs the new binary and runs `bd bootstrap`. That is a coordinated, human-sequenced,
multi-machine operation sitting in our critical path. Worse, the upgrade is sometimes not
available at all: br's current main targets schema 17 and its reviewed migration accepts only
13-to-17 and 14-to-17, so a 0.2.19 database has no supported path forward from schema 16. A
dependency we cannot upgrade, and cannot decline to upgrade, is not a dependency we manage.

The compounding factor is that beads owns **our state** - every phase derivation, gate,
checkpoint, dependency edge, decision and run record. A library that owns no state can be swapped
in an afternoon; a product that owns the state cannot be swapped at all without a migration.

## The rule

**No third-party product may own basicly's state.** Libraries and frameworks are permitted and
pinned. An optional extension - existing skills, language or technology guidelines - is permitted
and must stay optional.

## Classification of every current dependency

| Component | Class | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jinja2`, `jsonschema`, `pyyaml`, `ruamel.yaml`, `rich` | library | **Keep.** Pinned, semver, owns no state. The catalog stays YAML - the stdlib-has-no-YAML-parser problem is no longer forcing a move to TOML. |
| `uv` | tool | **Keep.** Versioned, replaceable, owns no state. |
| pre-commit framework | framework | **Keep.** Dispatches our hooks; owns no state. |
| node (markdownlint hook) | tool | **Keep**, but it is the weakest entry - it is the only one whose absence has actually broken a commit path on this machine, and it earns a re-examination on its own merits rather than under this rule. |
| Python 3.14+ | language runtime | **Keep.** Not a product. Whether the floor should drop is an adoption question, not this one. |
| **`br` / beads** | **product that owns our state** | **Remove.** This is the whole of the directive. Tracked by `basicly-vkh0`. |
| **`bv`** | **product** | **Remove.** Measured at 0 of 141 surfaces used (`basicly-vkh0.2`), so this is a deletion rather than a replacement. |

## Why this epic still exists rather than folding into vkh0

`vkh0` removes the one product we have. This epic is the **policy** that stops the next one
arriving, which is the part that outlives the migration: the rule above written down where an
agent proposing a dependency will read it, the classification kept current, and a gate that
refuses a new runtime dependency it cannot classify.

## Success Criteria

- The dependency rule is stated in the architecture reference, every current dependency is classified against it, `br` and `bv` are gone from the runtime path, and a check refuses a newly added runtime dependency that is not classifiable as a library or framework

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: When the harness loop runs end to end in a consumer repository, no third-party product is invoked or required. When a component is a library or a framework, it stays pinned and declared, and it owns no state. When a new runtime dependency is added without a recorded classification, a gate fails.

## Trigger

When a lane declares a scope glob that covers a configured append-only path, I want the preflight report to recognize that coverage the same way the landing does, so I can stop a false `contend:` line.

## Context

Found by the lane-B survey 2026-08-14.

```text
contention.py:61   path not in scopes.get(lane, ())     literal string membership
merge.py:942       merge._scope_covers                  decompose.globs_overlap
```

So a lane that declares `docs/**` or `*.md` covers a configured append-only `CHANGELOG.md` at the landing, and the preflight counts it as a lane that contends without declaring.

## Why it matters despite being advisory

Nothing refuses on this surface. The cost is a false `contend:` line. This repository records that an advisory `contend:` line is a finding an operator acts on: one such line named the exact collision under a green verdict and four hand-resolved rebases followed. A false one spends the same attention.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read the two scope tests side by side:

       rg -n 'path not in scopes.get' src/basicly/contention.py
       rg -n -A8 'def _scope_covers' src/basicly/merge.py

   `contention.append_only_report` asks `path not in scopes.get(lane, ())` - literal string
   membership against the lane's declared entries. `merge._scope_covers` asks
   `decompose.globs_overlap(path, glob)`. A lane declaring `docs/**` or `*.md` satisfies the
   second and fails the first.
2. Note the report is inert on this repo as configured, so the case has to supply a path:

       rg -n '^append_only_paths' basicly.toml

   Observed 2026-08-19: `append_only_paths = []`, and `append_only_report` returns its
   "no append-only path declared" line for an empty list before it reaches the membership
   test. So the reproduction belongs in `tests/test_contention.py` against a fixture repo
   that configures `append_only_paths = ["CHANGELOG.md"]`, not against this checkout.
3. In that fixture, give two lanes a `## Scope`: one declaring the glob `*.md` on its own
   backticked line, one declaring nothing that covers `CHANGELOG.md`. Call
   `contention.append_only_report` with both lanes.
4. Read the returned lines.

Observed: both lanes appear in the `... lane(s) will each append to `CHANGELOG.md` and none
declares it` line, so the report names a lane that did declare it and the operator reads a
`contend:` line that is false.
Expected: the lane whose declared glob covers the path is excluded from the count, on the
same glob test the landing uses. The function's own docstring already states that intent -
"A lane that *declares* the path in its own `## Scope` is left out of the count" - so this is
the docstring's rule failing on a glob, not a behaviour change.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/contention.py`
- `tests/test_contention.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_contention.py -q` with a new case that declares `*.md` against `CHANGELOG.md`.

payload.value: When a lane declares a scope glob that covers a configured append-only path, the preflight report does not count that lane as contending. When no lane declares coverage, the report stays unchanged.

## Trigger

When a unit under an L3 autonomy grant still has an outstanding `validate-as-consumer` gate, I want the ship-delegation check to name it as a violation, so I can close the second layer that today stays silent.

## Context

`basicly-u2hl.54.1` made `validate-as-consumer` a required gate for a unit whose recorded
`[harness-classification]` marker names L3. The augmentation is applied at
`loop_state.read_node_state` and at `cli._cmd_policy_gate`, so the derived phase and
`basicly policy gate` both answer against the unit own required set.

`policy._ship_delegation_violations` (`policy.py:2264`) is the third caller of
`policy.gate_status` and was deliberately left on the base config, because that function
is the L3 ship-delegation refusal rather than the loop own ladder, and `policy.py` sits at
**10 tokens of headroom** under the module-size ratchet (32,472 of a frozen 32,482), so

## Trigger

When feature pressure adds work faster than a one-off architecture audit can track, I want a mechanism that drains the backlog and bounds the whole tree, so I can stop the review from becoming a second unmanaged backlog.

## Goal

Cut unnecessary complexity, dead code and ambiguous concepts out of basicly, and leave behind the deterministic and non-deterministic mechanisms that make a one-off pass unnecessary ever again.

## Why the mechanism half is not optional

**This analysis has already been run once.** `basicly-tcmy` is the 2026-08-01 architecture and code review: three read-only passes over the engine, the projector and the instruction catalog. Its own baseline reads *43 modules in a six-tier DAG*. Measured 2026-08-14: **86 modules, 42,966 lines**, and **13 of its children are still open**.

So a read-only pass that emits a prioritised list is a thing this repo can already produce. What it cannot do is **drain the list against feature pressure**. Commissioning a second audit without the draining mechanism buys a second backlog with the same fate, which is why pass 2 below is a precondition of the work being worth paying for rather than a follow-on.

The supporting measurement: `src/basicly/` went **36,641 to 42,966 lines in one week** with the module-size ratchet, the comment-density ratchet, the noqa ratchet, vulture, lint-imports and wired-or-deleted all live and green. **A ratchet bounds a file. Nothing bounds the tree.**

## The three passes

**Pass 0 - re-verify the inherited backlog.** Take `basicly-tcmy`'s 13 open children against today's tree and classify each done, moot, still-real or worse, with the check that decides it. A finding cites a `path:line` and code moves; an unverified inherited finding is a claim, not evidence. Adding new findings on top of an unverified backlog is how you get two backlogs.

**Pass 1 - the survey.** The `architect` role, at its declared maximum tier, over the tree. Output is a dependency-ordered backlog shaped so the plan gate admits it unchanged, so the loop can dispatch it without translation.

Scope exclusions, each with a reason rather than an exemption:

- `br.py` and the 32 `run_br` call sites across 12 modules - they leave the tree at the tracker flip (`basicly-u4xu`). Auditing a scheduled deletion spends budget the calendar already spends.
- `runner.py`'s subprocess dispatch path - replaced by `basicly-xjd2`.
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/` - no frozen surface, no declared schema, no cache decision. An audit needs a specification to judge against, and `work-tracker.md` section 7 now records that one does not exist.

**Pass 2 - the mechanisms.** Deterministic and non-deterministic, both, because each covers what the other cannot: a gate binds without judgement and cannot read intent; a role judges and cannot bind.

Non-deterministic, all already specified and none of them new inventions:

- `basicly-feje` - map `reviewer` to a phase so the per-lens adversarial review runs on every lane instead of never.
- `basicly-u2hl.22` - derive `change-shape` from an AST. This is the call-chain instrument; without it "a call chain that does not make sense" is a thing only a human notices.
- RETROSPECTIVE as a state with the special-cause trigger, so the system decides *when* a structural finding is worth acting on instead of tampering on every single occurrence.

Deterministic:

- `basicly-u2hl.27` - the controller and actuator. Set point, four sensors and the dampener already exist; what is missing is the thing that selects the next target and dispatches it. **This is the bead that decides whether any of the rest lands.**
- A tree-level size budget, because the per-file ratchets were all green through a 17%-in-one-week growth.
- `basicly-r343` - the dead-code gate reads English prose in a schema as a field reference, so it can pass a real finding.
- `basicly-plhx` - the agent schema lets a role ship with no tier, so D26's routing rule can be defeated silently.
- `basicly-a3yi` - resolve a declared tier into the projected surface, so a tier declaration reaches a spawn at all.

## Ranking rule for the backlog

Dependency order, not severity order. Severity decides what is in; dependency decides what is next. The finding that unblocks the most other findings goes first.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: When pass 0 completes, each of `basicly-tcmy`'s open children carries a recorded verdict of done, moot, still-real or worse, with the command that decided it. When pass 1 completes, every emitted backlog item passes the plan gate unchanged, carries the measurement that found it, and the backlog is ordered by dependency. When pass 2 completes, a controller selects and dispatches the next remediation target without a human choosing it, and a tree-level growth signal exists that the per-file ratchets cannot mask.

## Trigger

When the fragment source vocabulary changes, I want the schema and the code to share one named constant, so I can let a tripwire catch the two sides drifting apart.

## Context

Left as a residual by the `basicly-3oxp` lane 2026-08-14, which tripwired five of the six schema and
Python vocabulary pairs and could not reach the sixth without a source change outside its scope.

Two schemas declare the same two-value vocabulary:

```text
.basicly/core/schemas/fragment.schema.json   "source": {"enum": ["core", "user"]}
.basicly/core/schemas/agent.schema.json      "source": {"enum": ["core", "user"]}
src/basicly/loader.py:256                    if fragment.source not in {"core", "user"}:
```

The Python side is an **inline set literal inside a guard**, not a named constant, so there is nothing
for a tripwire to import and compare against. The pair is the only one of six that stays uncovered,
and the new module's docstring records the gap so it does not read as covered.

## Why the one-line change is the whole fix

Hoist the literal to a module constant - `SOURCES = frozenset({"core", "user"})` - and use it at that
guard. `tests/test_schema_vocabularies.py` then takes the pair as a sixth row in its `SCHEMA_ENUMS`
table and both mutation directions become checkable, exactly as the other five already are.

This is the same defect class the lane's own bead names and that this repository has now paid for
four times in one session: two declarations of one vocabulary that can drift apart silently. A
tripwire on five pairs and nothing on the sixth reads as covered, which is worse than no tripwire at
all.

## A second, differently shaped restatement the bead never named

All four schemas - `fragment`, `skill`, `agent` and `block` - declare
`"schema_version": {"const": 1}` against `schema.SOURCE_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1`. Same two-declaration
shape, but a **const rather than an enum**, so it needs a differently shaped row than `SCHEMA_ENUMS`
carries. Both halves belong in this bead because the fix is one table gaining two kinds of row.

## Acceptance

- When `loader` declares the fragment source vocabulary, then it names one constant and the guard
  reads it, with no inline set literal left at that site.
- When `tests/test_schema_vocabularies.py` runs, then the `source` pair is compared in both
  directions like the other five.
- When any of the four schemas restates `schema_version`, then a check compares it against
  `schema.SOURCE_SCHEMA_VERSION` and fails if they disagree.
- When a member is added to either side of any pair without the other, then the test fails - proven
  by mutation in both directions, with each probe reverted by hand.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loader.py`
- `tests/test_loader.py`
- `tests/test_schema_vocabularies.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_schema_vocabularies.py -q` passes with six enum rows and four
`schema_version` rows; then add `zzprobe` to one side of each new pair, read the failure, and revert
by hand. Paste both failures - a tripwire nobody has watched fail is a claim.

## Headroom, measured at main 866b821

`tests/test_schema_vocabularies.py` is new and well under the 4000-token cap. `loader.py` is not
frozen for size. Measure before writing prose anyway; a lane today lost that argument twice.

## Trigger

When two lanes each change a declared generated block by the same amount, I want the block to rebuild from the merged tree on every landing, so I can stop a clean auto-merge from leaving a silently wrong count.

## Context

Found 2026-08-14 when lane `basicly-2j5a` bounced on `docs-claims` at its landing, hours after
`basicly-3w51` shipped the per-path rebuild that exists to prevent exactly that bounce.

The rebuild is triggered by a **rebase conflict**. Two lanes that each increment the same counter to
the same value produce **identical text**, so git auto-merges them cleanly, no conflict is raised, the
rebuild never fires, and the merged value is wrong by one.

Observed, not reasoned:

```text
base after basicly-3oxp landed          Test files | 163
lane basicly-2j5a's own block            Test files | 163   (correct in its pre-rebase tree)
after the rebase, no conflict raised     Test files | 163
the true value with both files present               164
```

The landing then failed on `docs-claims`, and regenerating in the rebased worktree produced 164.

## What worked and what did not, stated separately

**The gate failed safe.** `docs-claims` refused the landing rather than committing a false count, which
is the behaviour that matters most. Nothing wrong reached main.

**The mechanism did not do its job.** `basicly-3w51` exists so a lane does not bounce on a file it did
not author. Here the lane bounced anyway, and a human had to regenerate the block by hand and commit
it. That is the cost `3w51` was bought to remove, and it returns for every pair of lanes that move a
counter by the same amount - which for a counter incremented by one is the *common* case, not the rare
one.

## Why the conflict trigger is the wrong predicate

A conflict means the two sides disagree textually. What a generated block actually needs is a
rebuild whenever **its inputs changed**, and its inputs are the tree, not the file. Two lanes each
adding one test file change the input twice while writing the same text once.

So the predicate wants to be *the path is declared generated and this landing touched anything its
command reads*, or more simply: rebuild a declared generated path on every landing, unconditionally.
The command is deterministic and cheap - `docs_claims.py --fix --block` runs in well under a second -
so an unconditional rebuild costs almost nothing and removes a whole class of near-miss.

Note the tension to resolve rather than assume: `3w51` deliberately scoped the rebuild to conflicts
because the file is only **partly** generated and discarding both sides of the whole path would
destroy hand-authored prose. An unconditional rebuild must therefore stay block-scoped, which
`--block` already makes possible. That is why this is filed as a change to the trigger and not to the
resolution.

## Acceptance

- When a landing rebases a lane that changed a declared generated path, then the path is rebuilt from
  the merged tree regardless of whether the rebase raised a conflict.
- When two lanes each add one test file and land in sequence, then the second landing produces the
  true count without a human regenerating anything.
- When a rebuild runs, then hand-authored prose outside the marked block is unchanged, asserted
  against a lane that edited both.
- When the rebuild command fails or leaves a conflict marker, then the landing still bounces to the
  lane, as it does today.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/rebase.py`
- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `tests/test_rebase.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

## Warning

`tests/test_rebase.py` sits at exactly the 4000-token cap with zero headroom and is unfrozen -
`basicly-e2mz.2` is filed against precisely that. Sequence this after it, or expect the gate to refuse
the first line you add.

## Demonstration

Land two lanes that each add one test file, in sequence, with no human intervention between them, and
read the generated block on main: it must equal the tree. Then land a lane that edits the
hand-authored prose beside the block and confirm the edit survives.

When the board's wall mode attaches to a live source, I want requirement 10 amended to permit it while it shows its own age and never claims real time, so I can keep the original overclaim guard intact.

real-time* - with the reason recorded at the site: *"A generated Mermaid/DOT graph and a static HTML

Requirement 10 stays exactly as written. One sentence is added permitting a live-attached mode, under
two conditions that keep the original overclaim guard intact:

## Trigger

When `wired_or_deleted.py` cannot reach the module-size cap by one more extraction, I want its three finding surfaces to share one substrate, so I can split the gate without creating an import cycle.

## Context

Split out of `basicly-kr7t` by owner decision 2026-08-14, after a lane proved the cap unreachable in
one cut.

`kr7t` now removes the r343 waiver and lands the reference-index extraction near 5,022 tokens. **This
bead reaches the 4,000-token cap**, and it needs a different shape than an extraction.

## Why one more extraction cannot do it

`field_findings`, `command_findings` and `suppression_findings` each construct `Finding`, which is the
gate's output vocabulary. Moving any one into its own module makes
`wired_or_deleted -> surface -> wired_or_deleted`, and the gate runs as `__main__`, so the cycle is
real rather than a lint opinion. Moving `Finding` into a surface module instead is a token shuffle
with no nameable responsibility behind it.

So the cut is: **`Finding` and `WiringError` into a shared substrate**, each of the three surfaces
becomes its own module, and `wired_or_deleted.py` is left as baseline plus rule plus `main`.

## The floor this has to clear, measured

The residual gate module cannot be all prose. Its docstring is 938 tokens at essentially 100 percent
prose and `BASELINE` is 1,121 tokens at 48.7 percent - a 1,483-token prose floor - so it needs **at
least 1,940 tokens of content below 27 percent prose** beside them or it fails the comment-density cap
even after passing module-size. Design against that number rather than discovering it.

## The trap carried over from kr7t

`basicly.d/basicly-r343.toml` carries both `".scripts/wired_or_deleted.py" = -6554` and
`count_delta = 1`. Dropping only the `count_delta` leaves the path with **no frozen entry at all**, and
any result over 4,000 then fails `_over_cap` immediately. Both go together or neither does.

## Acceptance

- When `check_module_size.py` runs, then `.scripts/wired_or_deleted.py` and every module split out of
  it are at or under the 4,000-token cap with no waiver.
- When `check_comment_density.py` runs, then each of those modules is under the 50 percent cap with no
  waiver, or carries one whose reason is cohesion and says so.
- When `wired_or_deleted.py` runs before and after, then it reports the same finding count from the
  same baseline, proven by mutation on each of the three surfaces.
- When the split lands, then no module imports back into `wired_or_deleted`, asserted rather than
  reasoned.

## Scope

- `.scripts/wired_or_deleted.py`
- three or four new modules under `.scripts/`
- `basicly.d/basicly-r343.toml`
- `pyproject.toml`
- `tests/test_wired_or_deleted.py`
- `tests/test_verify.py`
- a test module per new module

## Depends on

`basicly-kr7t`, which removes the waiver and must not find this file changed underneath it.

## Demonstration

`uv run python .scripts/wired_or_deleted.py` reports the same count as before; `check_module_size.py`
and `check_comment_density.py` both report one fewer waiver; `uv run pytest -q` green.

## Trigger

When a lane writes only the bead-named files the harness itself requires, I want the scope check to recognize its own convention, so I can stop a false violation from burying a real one.

## Steps to Reproduce

```
br comments list basicly-4f5g --json | rg scope-violation
br comments list basicly-0p8n --json | rg scope-violation
```

Observed, measured over the three lanes of session `basicly-u2hl:f9c58c11` on 2026-08-15 -
**3 of 3 lanes recorded a scope violation**, and two of them name an artifact the harness
itself requires that lane to write:

```
4f5g   basicly.d/basicly-4f5g.toml, tests/test_cli_loop.py, tests/test_loop.py
0p8n   changelog.d/basicly-0p8n.added.md, src/basicly/cli.py, tests/test_claude_settings.py
```

Expected - a lane is not reported for writing the file the engine told it to write.

## Context

`basicly.d/<bead-id>.toml` and `changelog.d/<bead-id>.<category>.md` are this repo own
per-lane conventions, introduced by `basicly-4746` and `basicly-ef7t` precisely so two lanes
can never write one file. They are named for the bead, so by construction they appear in no
bead `## Scope` - the same "a path every lane writes and no bead declares" class that
`[worktree] append_only_paths` exists for, except these need no serializing because each is
already bead-unique.

The cost is not a wrong landing - section 12.6 records an out-of-scope path and lands it, which
is correct. The cost is that the marker fires on every lane whatever the lane did, so a reader
learns to skip it, and the genuine finding in the same session is buried beside two false ones.
`tcmy.19` extracted a new module and repointed two callers at it - six undeclared paths that a
reviewer should see - and it reads identically to `4f5g` writing its own config fragment.

A gate that reports on every run reports nothing.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

## Trigger

When the supervisor selects more lanes than it provisions, I want the pass to name the withheld lane and the rule that withheld it, so I can tell a deliberate refusal from a defect.

## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run basicly loop supervise basicly-u2hl --label u2hl-pass-2
rg "^(wip|routed):" <the pass log>
```

Observed, two passes on 2026-08-15:

```
pass 1  wip: 0/5 unlanded downstream of build; 2 lane(s) admitted
        routed: provisioned 2 of 3 lane(s) selected by label
pass 2  wip: 0/5 unlanded downstream of build; 1 lane(s) admitted
        routed: provisioned 1 of 2 lane(s) selected by label
```

Both passes had **zero** work in flight against a headroom of five, and both left a
selected lane unprovisioned with no line saying why. Pass 2 then provisioned the
remaining lane on a later tick, after the first had shipped - so the two lanes ran
serially despite disjoint declared scopes and a wholly empty WIP bound.

Expected - when a selected lane is not provisioned, the pass says which lane and on
what rule.

## Why this is worth a bead rather than a shrug

The visible cost is throughput: pass 2 was two lanes with no scope overlap and it ran
them one after the other, so the pass took the sum rather than the maximum.

The invisible cost is worse and it is what happened here. A reader who sees
"provisioned 1 of 2" cannot tell a deliberate refusal from a defect, so the first
reading of pass 1 attributed it to `basicly-0p8n` being a `feature` and therefore not
a leaf track - which was true of that bead and does not explain pass 2, where both
`ho3t` and `u2hl.30` are leaf types with a readable `## Scope`. One plausible cause
was tested and refuted: `br blocked` does **not** propagate a blocked parent to its
children - measured, 45 entries against 32 with a real open blocks-edge, and every one
of the 13 extra is an epic with open children, with zero false negatives. So the cause
is still unknown, and that is the point.

`wip.py:169` admits `ready[:headroom]`, so the remainder is upstream of the WIP bound
in whatever produces `ready`. The line already prints on the admitted path
deliberately (`wip.py:105`); it needs to print on the withheld one too.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/wip.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given a pass that selected N lanes by label and provisioned fewer when the `routed:` line
  prints then it names each lane it did not provision and the rule that withheld it, so a
  deliberate refusal is distinguishable from a defect.
- Given the WIP bound withheld a lane when the pass reports then `wip.WipAdmission.coverage`
  prints the withheld ids on the *withheld* path, as it already does on the admitted one.
- Given two selected lanes with disjoint declared scopes and zero work in flight against a
  headroom of five when the pass ticks then both are provisioned in the same pass, or the
  output names the rule that stopped the second - the pass must not silently take the sum of
  two lanes where it could take the maximum.
- Given a pass in which every selected lane was provisioned then no reason line prints, so the
  new output is news rather than noise.
- Given the cause of the shortfall is not yet known then the change reports the rule the code
  actually applied rather than asserting a diagnosis - a wrong reason is worse than the
  current silence.
- Demonstrated by: `uv run basicly loop supervise <root> --label <label>` followed by
  `rg "^(wip|routed):" <pass log>`, with a named reason present for every lane in the gap
  between selected and provisioned, against the two 2026-08-15 passes above as the control
  that print no reason at all.

payload.value: When a pass selects lanes by label and provisions fewer, the `routed:` line names each unprovisioned lane and the rule that withheld it. When the WIP bound withholds a lane, `wip.WipAdmission.coverage` prints the withheld ids on the withheld path, as it already does on the admitted path. When every selected lane is provisioned, no reason line prints; when two selected lanes have disjoint scopes and headroom for both, both are provisioned in the same pass, or the output names the rule that stopped the second.

## Trigger

When a module sits exactly at the size cap with no freeze, I want the gate to report its headroom, so I can split it before it blocks the next lane that touches it.

## Context

Reported by the `basicly-3w51` lane 2026-08-14 and confirmed by hand at main after the merge.

```text
tests/test_rebase.py    tokens=4000   cap=4000   headroom=0
```

The module-size gate reports PASS, because 4000 is within the 4000-token cap. It is at the cap
exactly, and it is **not frozen** — so there is no baseline to fall back on. The next line added to
that file fails `module-size` outright, and the failure lands on whoever touches `rebase` next
rather than on whoever filled it.

## Why this is not the ordinary ratchet obligation

A frozen module above the cap may only shrink, and the first touch below 2x the cap must bring it
under. Both rules give the next author a payable move. A file resting on the cap with no freeze
gives none: it is green today and red on the next character, with nothing in the gate output saying
so. `module-size` prints a count of modules within cap or baseline; it does not print headroom, so a
file at zero is indistinguishable from one at two thousand.

Two separable pieces of work, and the second is the one that generalises.

## Acceptance

- When `tests/test_rebase.py` is split along a nameable responsibility, then each part is under the
  cap with room to add a test, and no assertion or fixture is deleted to buy the room.
- When `module-size` runs, then it names any tracked module whose headroom against its cap or its
  frozen baseline is below a declared threshold, so a file about to block the next lane is visible
  before it blocks one.
- When the headroom report exists, then it reports rather than blocks, because it has no firing
  history yet.

## Scope

- `tests/test_rebase.py`
- a new test module under `tests/`
- `.scripts/check_module_size.py`
- `tests/test_check_module_size.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run python .scripts/check_module_size.py` prints a headroom line naming every module below the
threshold, and adding one assertion to each split part of `tests/test_rebase.py` passes the gate.

## Note on the population this belongs to

Measured at main on 2026-08-14, three other modules sit at or near zero: `tests/test_decompose.py`
0 against a frozen 28885, `src/basicly/policy.py` 9 against 32482, `src/basicly/decompose.py` 11
against 24498. Two lanes in this session each had to cut their own added prose to land, and one
moved its regression test to a different file because the natural home had 1 token free. That is the
recurring shape, not a single file.

payload.value: When `tests/test_rebase.py` is split along a nameable responsibility, each part stays under the cap with room for one more test, and no assertion or fixture is deleted to make room. When `module-size` runs, it names any tracked module whose headroom against its cap or frozen baseline is below a declared threshold. When the headroom report exists, it reports rather than blocks.

## Trigger

When code is inserted above a cited symbol, I want the citation to name the symbol rather than its line, so I can stop an unrelated edit from invalidating a true claim.

## Context

Filed 2026-08-15 after the gate `basicly-miqr` shipped that morning fired four times in
one afternoon, on one changeset, all from the same cause.

## Observed

A single change adding 18 lines to `src/basicly/loop.py` invalidated **20 citations** across
`docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` and `docs/requirements/factory-loop.md`. Trimming a
docstring in the same file later moved two of them back and invalidated two more. None of
the underlying claims became false: every one still named the right symbol.

## The gate is right and the citation form is the defect

`check_docs_citations.py` already resolves the symbol - its own failure text reads
`outside the symbol named here - `foreign_dirt` is at :509`. So it knows the answer it is
asking the author to write down. A `file.py:line` citation is a claim that decays on every
insertion above it, while `file.py::symbol` would not.

Two rules it already enforces stay exactly as they are: a cited line must be live code, and
a cited line must fall inside the symbol named beside it. A symbol form satisfies both by
construction and removes the churn.

## Why the churn is worse than noise

Bulk-fixing them invites the failure the standing constraints already name. A fixer written
from the gate output rewrote `loop.py:1637` to `loop.py:749` because two citations shared one
document line and the regex took the first suggestion. The wrong number was caught by hand,
which is the audit the "a bulk find-replace needs a line-by-line audit" rule requires - and
the reason to remove the need for the fixer rather than to improve it.

## Not a request to weaken the gate

The one real correction found in the same afternoon is the argument for keeping it: the plan
cited `loop.dispatch_prompt` at a line, and that symbol had moved to `dispatch_brief`
entirely. A symbol-form citation would have failed on the missing symbol rather than
silently pointing at whatever now occupies the line.

## Scope

- `.scripts/check_docs_citations.py`
- `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md`
- `docs/requirements/factory-loop.md`
- `tests/test_check_docs_citations.py`

payload.value: When a document cites a symbol and code is inserted above that symbol, the citation stays valid because it names the symbol rather than its line. ## Trigger

When a projected agent definition changes after a session has started, I want the dispatch to carry the new definition or the harness to say it cannot, so I can stop a roster change from staying silently invisible.

## Context

`docs/requirements/factory-loop.md` records, as a measured finding dated 2026-08-09,
that agent definitions hot-reload and are not read once at process start, with two
named exceptions. That claim does not hold for the path the engine and an operator
actually use.

Measured 2026-08-16. `.basicly/core/agents/architect/agent.yaml` gained `Write` and
`Edit`; `basicly agents-build` wrote `.claude/agents/architect.md` and
`.github/agents/architect.agent.md`, and the projected frontmatter carries
`tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write, Edit`. A dispatch immediately afterwards
reported its live tool list as `Read, Bash` and refused the task it had been given.

## Why this matters beyond one dispatch

The catalog is the source and the projection is the delivery, so a projection that a
running host ignores makes every roster change invisible until a restart nobody
schedules. It is also the second instance of the shape this repo keeps paying for: a
capability asserted in a document, believed, and never probed.

## What is not established

Whether the stale registry is the host's or this harness's, and whether the
2026-08-09 measurement was wrong then or is stale now - it pinned no version, which
is the same defect `basicly-wbsz.3` was filed for.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a session that is already running, change a projected agent's capability at the
   catalog source - for example add `Write` and `Edit` to the `tools` of
   `.basicly/core/agents/architect/agent.yaml`.
2. Project it and confirm the projection landed:

       uv run basicly agents-build
       rg -n '^tools:' .claude/agents/architect.md .github/agents/architect.agent.md

3. Without restarting the host process, dispatch that role and ask it to report its own
   tool list and to perform an edit.
4. Compare the live tool list against the frontmatter from step 2.
5. Probe the harness for any code that notices the difference:

       rg -n 'stale_registry' tests/test_roles.py
       rg -n 'def ' src/basicly/roles.py

Observed - this record's measurement 2026-08-16: step 2's frontmatter read
`tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write, Edit`, and the dispatch in step 3 reported its live
tool list as `Read, Bash` and refused the task it had been given. Step 5's first command
returns nothing; **its positive control is the second command**, which lists six functions
in `roles.py` (`role_for_phase`, `lens_dispatches`, `role_is_available`, `resolve_role`,
`resolve_named_role`) - so `roles.py` is readable and the module simply carries no
registry-freshness check. Re-checked 2026-08-19: `rg -c 'def test_' tests/test_roles.py`
returns 17 tests and none of them matches `stale_registry`, so the gap is an absence rather
than a bad probe, and the projected frontmatter still reads
`tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write, Edit`.

Expected: either the dispatch carries the definition that is on disk at dispatch time, or
the harness reports that it cannot and names the process boundary as the reason - a roster
change must not be silently invisible.

- `docs/requirements/factory-loop.md`
- `src/basicly/roles.py`
- `tests/test_roles.py`

## Working Set

  names that role then either the dispatch carries the new definition or the harness
  reports that it cannot - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_roles.py -k stale_registry -q`

## Trigger

When a tracked file changes during a failing commit gate because of a concurrent writer, I want `basicly commit` to name that file as concurrently modified, so I can stop losing time chasing the wrong hook.

## Context

`pre-commit` snapshots the working tree before each hook and compares it after. A file
that changed during a hook is reported as **modified by that hook**. A concurrent
writer is indistinguishable from a hook write, so the blame lands on whichever hook was
running when the write arrived.

Measured 2026-08-16. Three commits in a row failed with
`catalog-lint: files were modified by this hook`, while `catalog lint: OK` printed in
the same output. A whole-tree probe cleared the command:

```
git ls-files -z | xargs -0 md5sum | sort > before
uv run basicly catalog lint
git ls-files -z | xargs -0 md5sum | sort > after
diff before after   ->  no output
```

The real writer was a background agent editing `docs/architecture/architecture.md`.
Its diff went from 416 to 528 insertions between the second and third attempts, so it
wrote inside the commit window. An hour went into the wrong hook.

## Why the framework cannot answer this and we can

`pre-commit` has no way to tell a hook's write from anybody else's, and it is not ours
to change. `basicly commit` already wraps `git commit`, so it is the one place that can
snapshot the tracked tree before the gate and compare after a failure. A file that
changed but is touched by no hook is a concurrent modification, and saying so turns an
hour of hunting into one line.

Post-hoc diagnosis on failure only. Not a refusal, and not a pre-flight heuristic on
file age - a human editing in another window is a false positive, and a gate that cries
wolf gets waived.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Stage a commit in this repo and start it through the wrapper:

       uv run basicly commit ...

2. While the gate is running, have a second process write to any tracked file the commit
   does not touch - for example append a line to `docs/architecture/architecture.md`.
3. Read the failure. `pre-commit` snapshots the tree before each hook and compares it
   after, so it reports `<hook-id>: files were modified by this hook` naming whichever hook
   happened to be running when the write arrived.
4. Clear the named hook by hand, which is the step that costs the time:

       git ls-files -z | xargs -0 md5sum | sort > before
       uv run basicly catalog lint
       git ls-files -z | xargs -0 md5sum | sort > after
       diff before after

5. Probe `basicly commit` for anything that would have said so:

       rg -n 'concurrent' src/basicly/commit.py tests/test_commit.py
       rg -c 'hook' src/basicly/commit.py

Observed - this record's measurement 2026-08-16: three commits in a row failed with
`catalog-lint: files were modified by this hook` while `catalog lint: OK` printed in the same
output, step 4's `diff` produced no output, and the real writer was a background agent whose
diff on `architecture.md` grew from 416 to 528 insertions between the second and third
attempts. An hour went into the wrong hook. Step 5, re-run 2026-08-19: the first command
returns nothing. **Its positive control is the second command**, which returns 15 `hook`
matches in a 586-line `commit.py`, and `grep -c 'def test_' tests/test_commit.py` returns 35
- both files exist and are searched, so the zero is an absence.

Expected: when a tracked file changed during a failing gate and no hook is configured to
touch it, `basicly commit` names that file as concurrently modified, post-hoc and on failure
only. When nothing changed, it says nothing about concurrency.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/commit.py`
- `tests/test_commit.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/commit.py`
- `tests/test_commit.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_commit.py -k concurrent -q`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given a tracked file changes while the commit gate runs when the commit fails then
  the output names that file as concurrently modified rather than leaving the hook
  blamed - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_commit.py -k concurrent -q`
- Given no file changes during a failing gate then the output says nothing about
  concurrency - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_commit.py -k concurrent -q`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: When a tracked file changes while the commit gate runs and the commit fails, the output names that file as concurrently modified rather than leaving the hook blamed. When no file changes during a failing gate, the output says nothing about concurrency.

## Trigger

When architecture section 30 describes where the curator and the retrospector run under a supervised pass, I want the text to match what the code does, so I can stop a reader from looking for a driver that is not in the picture.

## The defect

`docs/architecture/architecture.md` §30 *Roles at dispatch* carries this as the first of two
caveats:

> The curator and the retrospector are both inert on the supervised landing pass, which has
> no watchdog and no stream meter of its own. Under the supervisor they run only after the
> ship approval, on the interactive driver.

The first sentence holds. **The second does not.** Under the supervisor, both roles run on the
supervisor's own process after it approves the ship itself, and the driver the supervisor uses
to get there cannot switch them off even in principle - `loop.run_until_blocked` takes no
`repair_dispatch` parameter, so the ship advance runs with `advance`'s default of `True`.

So the text sends a reader looking for an interactive driver that is not in the picture, on
the one path where an unmetered dispatch actually happens.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read the claim:

       rg -n -A3 'inert on the supervised landing pass' docs/architecture/architecture.md

2. Read the two dispatches the claim is about, and the flag that gates each:

       rg -n -A3 'def _dispatch_curation' src/basicly/loop.py
       rg -n 'if root is None or not ctx.repair_dispatch' src/basicly/loop.py

3. Read what the supervisor passes on each of its two advances:

       rg -n 'loop.advance\(|loop.run_until_blocked\(' src/basicly/supervise.py

4. Read whether the second of those can pass the flag at all:

       rg -n -A9 'def run_until_blocked' src/basicly/loop.py

5. Confirm which process approved the ship on a real supervised pass: read the pass log for
   the `ship pending - the live L3 grant delegates it` preflight line and then check the
   parent process of the curator's dispatch.

Observed, verified in code 2026-08-19 at main 9534ca05:

- `supervise._land_green` passes `repair_dispatch=False` to the build->verify
  `loop.advance` (`src/basicly/supervise.py:3971`), with a comment giving exactly the reason
  the architecture text gives. That is sentence one, and it is correct.
- Once `policy.approve_checkpoint_guarded(..., interactive=False, grant_root=session.root_issue)`
  approves - which an L3 grant does, with no human in it - the same function ships through
  `loop.run_until_blocked(repo_root, outcome.issue_id, grant_root=session.root_issue)`
  (`supervise.py:3998`). `supervise.advance_parked` reaches the same driver.
- `loop.run_until_blocked` has **no** `repair_dispatch` parameter and calls
  `advance(repo_root, issue_id, config=..., inputs=..., grant_root=...)`, so
  `repair_dispatch` takes its default `True`. `loop._dispatch_curation` and
  `loop._retrospective` are gated only on that flag, so both fire - in the supervisor
  process.
- The behavioural half was already observed 2026-08-16 on a supervised pass over
  `basicly-e2mz`: after `basicly-e2mz.13` landed, the curator was dispatched with the
  supervisor process itself as its parent, and preflight had reported
  `ship pending - the live L3 grant delegates it`.

Expected: §30 states that the supervisor dispatches the curator and the retrospector itself
once a grant delegates the ship approval, names the driver that does it, and does not claim an
interactive driver is required.

## Scope

- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given `docs/architecture/architecture.md` §30 is read at the *Roles at dispatch* caveats
  when it describes where the curator and the retrospector run under a supervised pass, then
  it states that the supervisor dispatches them itself once a grant delegates the ship
  approval, and it does not claim an interactive driver is required.
- Given the corrected text then it distinguishes the build->verify landing, which passes
  `repair_dispatch=False`, from the ship advance, which cannot pass it - so a reader learns
  which of the supervisor's two advances is metered and which is not.
- Given the corrected text then every claim in it names the module and function a reader can
  check it against, rather than describing a driver.
- Demonstrated by: reading the edited section against
  `rg -n 'loop.advance\(|loop.run_until_blocked\(' src/basicly/supervise.py` and
  `rg -n -A9 'def run_until_blocked' src/basicly/loop.py`, with no sentence left that the
  two outputs contradict.

## Trigger

When an operator failure repeats because no gate refused it, I want the remedy to be a deterministic check rather than added prose, so I can stop the next lane from hitting the same wall.

## Context

On 2026-08-16 every lane failure in the session was operator error, not an engine defect. The engine refused correctly and named the cause every time. The owner asked for a remedy, and the remedy is not simply more prose in the always-on files.

This repository already states the hierarchy: git hooks are the deterministic floor, and guidance is what you use when a gate cannot express the check. The always-on baseline is also measured at 7014 to 7343 characters and is at its cap, so a new always-on rule costs something real and must earn it.

## The four failures and the tier each one belongs in

1. A stray 7.6 MB file under the tracker directory was committed by the tracker-state rollup, which stages the whole directory. CODE. Filed as basicly-vkh0.31.
2. The ignore list missed the file because it is a denylist of suffixes and the name ended `.recovered` rather than `.db`. CODE, same bead: stage known paths instead of relying on ignore rules.
3. `basicly loop run` on a child defaults the session root to the child, so a grant on the parent is never consulted, and the refusal does not name the `--root` flag that fixes it. Two dispatch attempts died on this. CODE: either default a child root to its parent, or name the flag in the refusal text.
4. A subagent was told to write its output into `docs/architecture/` inside the base checkout. An actively written file in the base checkout blocks every lane landing, and it blocked three. GUIDANCE: no gate can see the intent behind a subagent brief.

## What this bead must not become

A fragment that says be careful. Each item above either becomes a check that refuses the thing, or it does not land. Item 4 is the only guidance candidate, and it should be authored as a catalog source, never a hand-written discoverable markdown file, per the catalog-authoring rule.

## Sequencing

Run after the architecture rewrite is verified and swapped in. The rewrite renumbers sections that code cites, and doing both at once would tangle two unrelated diffs.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `.basicly/core/fragments/**`
- `tests/**`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: When each of the four named failures has its remedy landed, three are deterministic checks that refuse the failing input and name the cause, and the fourth is a catalog-authored guidance entry scoped to the narrowest tier that reaches the reader. When a proposed remedy is only prose advising more care, it is rejected and the record states why.

## Trigger

When a scope collision names a lane that has no commits and a clean tree, I want the landing gate to say it holds no work and to name the command that releases it, so I can stop losing a landing to an empty claim.

## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-08-16. `basicly-vkh0.32` was refused at the landing:

    [blocked] build -> build: basicly-vkh0.32 changed .importlinter, docs/plan/implementation-plan.md,
    src/basicly/br.py, src/basicly/edge_adoption.py, tests/test_edge_adoption.py,
    tests/test_tracker_cutover.py outside its declared scope
    (src/basicly/tracker_cutover.py, tests/test_tracker_adoption.py), and basicly-b2n2 declared
    that ground: the plan is wrong, not the merge.

Half of that refusal was correct and is not this bead: the scope declaration really was wrong, and the gate said so precisely.

The other half was a collision with a lane that had produced nothing:

    git log --oneline main..harness/basicly-b2n2 | wc -l    -> 0
    git -C <worktree> status --short | wc -l                -> 0

Zero commits ahead of main, clean worktree, sitting on a base from an earlier session. `basicly-b2n2` had held `src/basicly/br.py` and a worktree slot since before the session while writing no code.

Tearing the worktree down released the ground and the lane landed. Nothing was lost, because there was nothing to lose.

## The gap

The architecture defines live deliberately: "Live means the worktree session records on disk, not the tracker export." The reason is good and should not be reverted - a freshly provisioned lane is the one most likely to be mid-edit, and the export would not show it.

But presence of a worktree record is a weak proxy for occupancy. It cannot distinguish:

- a lane mid-edit with uncommitted work, which must hold its ground;
- a lane with commits, which must hold its ground;
- a lane with no commits and a clean tree, which is holding a claim and a concurrency slot and nothing else.

The third case cost a landing, a rework attempt, and an operator decision today. It also occupied one of five worktree slots, which separately blocked a dispatch earlier in the same session.

## What this is not

Not an argument for reading the tracker export instead. Not an argument for auto-reaping a lane: a human parked it for a reason, and deleting work is the one thing a scope gate must never do. A lane with no commits but a dirty tree is genuinely mid-edit and must keep its ground.

The remedy is discrimination and a better message, not eviction.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/contention.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: When a scope collision involves a lane that has no commits ahead of the base and no uncommitted changes, the landing gate names that lane as holding no work, and names the command that releases it. When a collision involves a lane that has commits or uncommitted changes, the refusal stays unchanged. When the preflight runs and a provisioned lane has no commits and a clean tree, it reports that lane as holding a slot without work.

## Trigger

When a quarter of the open backlog cannot be dispatched because it carries no acceptance criteria, I want one report that names every refused record and its reason, so I can stop probing hundreds of records by hand.

## Context

A quarter of the open backlog cannot be dispatched, and nothing says so until someone tries one bead at a time.

Measured 2026-08-17 over `.beads/issues.jsonl`, 221 open records:

| Population | Count |
| --- | --- |
| acceptance criteria in the structured field | 134 |
| field empty, but the description carries an `## Acceptance Criteria` heading | 32 |
| criteria nowhere at all | **55**, of which 52 are not epics |

The discriminator is proven rather than assumed, with one probe per population:

    basicly policy dor basicly-vkh0.36   ->  DoR: READY          (field populated)
    basicly policy dor basicly-e2mz.35   ->  DoR: READY          (heading in the description only)
    basicly policy dor basicly-y8el      ->  DoR: NOT READY - missing: ## Acceptance Criteria

So the heading in the description is sufficient and the field is not required. The 55 have neither, and every one of them stops at classify with the same refusal. 24 of them are priority 1.

The count is a floor rather than a ceiling: the readiness check answers more than the criteria question, so a record that passes this filter can still be refused for another missing section.

## Why it is worth a bead rather than an afternoon

Two reasons, and the second is the one that makes it a mechanism problem.

A dispatch on any of the 55 costs a worktree provisioning and an intake advance before the refusal, so the cost of the gap is paid per attempt rather than once.

And the readiness rules are not ours yet. `policy.definition_of_ready` spawns the external binary's `lint`, which is the first of the operations with no owned equivalent, and porting it is inside `basicly-wpc8.1`. Whoever owns those rules chooses whether the description heading keeps counting. That choice moves this number in either direction, so the report has to read the live rule rather than restate it.

## What to build

A report that names every open record the readiness check refuses, with the reason it gives, so the gap is one command rather than 221 probes. It reads the live check rather than re-implementing its rules.

Then the authoring pass itself, which is the improvement controller's kind of work: 52 small edits, each writing criteria for a record whose intent is already in its title and description.

## Contention to respect

Folding this into `basicly policy dor --all` would touch `src/basicly/policy.py` and `src/basicly/cli.py`. Both are inside the declared scope of open beads, `basicly-wpc8.1` and `basicly-wpc8`, so the report starts as a script instead. Adding a `[[verify.checks]]` entry touches `basicly.toml`, which `basicly-vkh0.29` declares and `basicly-vkh0.37` is amending, so sequence it after those rather than beside them.

## Scope

- `.scripts/report_readiness.py`
- `tests/test_report_readiness.py`

payload.value: When the readiness report runs, it names every open record the readiness check refuses and the reason each refusal gives, and it reads the live check rather than a restated copy of its rules. When a record passes the check, it does not appear in the report. When the authoring pass finishes, no non-epic open record is refused for missing acceptance criteria.

payload.value:

- [ ] The same write is refused, naming the changed field, when a later event changed a field it writes.

## Trigger

When a config entry overrides the copilot agent without restating deny_style, I want format_command to stop raising, so I can dispatch the overridden agent instead of failing every call.

## Context

Found 2026-07-31 while exercising basicly-kjc5.59 through `basicly runner dry-run`. Not caused by
that change - reproduced on base `main` with a config that names no tier at all.

`[[runner.agents]]` replaces a builtin wholesale by design, so an entry overriding `copilot`
that does not restate `deny_style` gets `deny_style = None`. But `_inject_copilot_deny_tools`
still injects the permissions.yaml deny list onto that spec, and `format_command` then raises
