## Trigger

When a lane is killed past its runner timeout and `commit.salvage` commits its worktree, I want the resulting commit subject to describe the bead's own work and type, so I can read `git log` and the changelog as an accurate record of what changed.

## Context

Observed 2026-08-06 landing `basicly-rupz`. Its lane hit the wall clock and `commit.salvage`
committed the worktree, which then merged to `main` verbatim as:

```
9607ff8 feat(runner): salvage the work a killed runner left uncommitted (basicly-rupz)
```

That subject describes `basicly-yvx9`'s feature - the salvage mechanism - not `rupz`'s work,
which was consuming the dispatch event stream. `commit.py:539` holds a module constant:

```python
SALVAGE_DESCRIPTION = "salvage the work a killed runner left uncommitted"
```

and `commit.py:596` passes it to `assemble` for every salvage, so every salvaged bead lands
under the same subject regardless of what it did.

## Why it is not cosmetic

The landing preserves individual commit subjects rather than squashing - `basicly-1lpo`
landed as `07f8c65 feat(supervise): fan a pass out over a label ...` because its salvage
refused and the commit was made by hand. So the wrong subject is permanent in `main`'s
history, and it is wrong on the two surfaces that read subjects as the record of what
changed: `git log` and the changelog fragment a lane writes.

It also mislabels the *type*. A salvage of a `docs`-only or `chore` bead still lands as
`feat(runner)`, so the subject asserts a scope and a type the diff does not support.

## Shape to consider

The bead title is already in hand at the salvage call site - `commit.salvage` takes `bead`.
Composing the subject from the bead's own title and type (the same source the
`conventional-commits` skill uses) makes the subject describe the work, and the salvage fact
belongs in the body, which `_salvage_body` already writes and a human already meets in
`git show`.

## Steps to Reproduce

Kill a metered lane past `runner_timeout` on any bead, let `commit.salvage` commit, then
read the subject: it names the salvage feature, not the bead.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: A salvaged commit's subject describes the bead's own work and carries the bead's own type and scope, not a fixed salvage description. The fact that a commit was a salvage is recorded in the commit body, not in the subject.

When a whole-repo reachability scan finds symbols with no production caller, some outright dead and some built but unwired despite being cited as a decision input in the docs, I want each one either wired to a real caller or deleted with its tests, so I can trust that a green dead-code gate means no unreferenced symbol remains.

## Context

Verified by whole-repo reachability scan over 594 non-binary files including catalog YAML, hooks, tests, docs and scripts.

Dead outright: `permissions.PERMISSION_TARGETS` (permissions.py:40) - exactly one occurrence repo-wide, its own definition. `policy.gate_from_unreliable_escalation` (policy.py:560) and its regex - tests only; tracked by the unreliable-escalation bead, delete here only if that bead resolves by dropping the offer. `PassSpendAdmission.unforecast` (supervise.py:1286) is always `()` from both constructors, so its UNBOUNDED coverage branch cannot fire. `cli.py:1756`'s `if args.usage_command != 'report'` guard is unreachable. `RunnerConfig.default_tier` (config.py:925) is stored but never read - `_apply_default_tier` already folds it onto every spec at load.

Built and unwired, cited by docs as a decision input: `run_record.landed_package_cost` (run_record.py:605) plus LandedCost and per_package - named as a prerequisite in architecture.md:1595, implementation-plan.md:447, agent-roster-design.md:218 and 459 and catalog-efficacy-design.md:385, but `basicly usage` exposes only report, forecast and tracker. Also `policy.should_escalate` (policy.py:485) - the n=2 rework predicate from §12.2, with callers instead comparing inline. Also `worktree.stale_sessions`.

Also here: the three renderer shims (renderers/claude.py, codex.py, copilot.py) are 11 lines each, byte-identical apart from a docstring, dispatched by importlib at cli.py:191 so invisible to the type checker. architecture.md:292 justifies the layer by per-target activation syntax that lives entirely in targets YAML and templates, not in these files.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/permissions.py`
- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/run_record.py`
- `src/basicly/worktree.py`
- `src/basicly/config.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `src/basicly/renderers/**`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given each named symbol when the change lands then it is either called from production or deleted together with its tests
- Given landed_package_cost when the docs name it as a decision input then either a command exposes it or the doc claims are struck
- Given the renderer dispatch when a target is rendered then no per-target Python shim exists that adds no behaviour
- Given the package after the change when the reachability scan is re-run then it reports no public symbol whose only references are its definition and its tests

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: Each named symbol with no production caller, other than `policy.gate_from_unreliable_escalation` which the record's own follow-up confirms has live callers, is wired to a caller or deleted together with its tests. Where a symbol is cited in a document as a decision input for scheduled work, either a command exposes it or the document's claim is struck. Since no existing gate reports "no public symbol whose only references are its definition and its tests", emptying the dead-code gate's allowlist of these symbols is the completion signal.

## Trigger

When an unexpected exception during a long `loop supervise` run prints only a one-line message with the location lost, I want the traceback to reach the operator behind a debug switch while the default output stays a one-line message, so I can diagnose a failure without losing the error detail.

## Context

`cli.py:4436` catches bare Exception, prints `Error: {exc}` and returns 1. `rg 'traceback|logging|BASICLY_DEBUG' src/basicly/` returns exactly one hit and it is a comment - there is no logger, no --traceback flag and no debug environment variable anywhere in the package.

So an AttributeError three frames into a two-hour `loop supervise` prints `Error: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'binding'` and the location is gone. CLAUDE.md's secure-coding rule is to not leak internal detail in user-facing errors, log it and return a generic message - this satisfies the first half and skips the second, so the detail is neither shown usefully nor retained.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_cli.py`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given an unexpected exception when the debug switch is set then the traceback reaches the operator
- Given the same exception when the switch is not set then the output is the existing one-line message and the exit code is unchanged

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: With the debug switch set, an unexpected exception's traceback reaches the operator. With the debug switch not set, the output stays the existing one-line message and the exit code stays unchanged.

## Trigger

When a declared scope glob matches a binary or very large tracked file, I want the working-set estimate to bound that file's contribution before it is decoded, so I can stop one large file from dominating a lane's size estimate.

## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from basicly import decompose
print(len(decompose._scope_files(Path('.'), ('.beads/**',))))
"
du -sh .beads
```

Observed - the glob matches the multi-hundred-megabyte tracker database and scope_read_cost reads it. Expected - a binary or oversized file contributes a bounded amount and does not dominate a lane's estimate.

## Context

`decompose.scope_read_cost` reads every matched file with `read_text(encoding='utf-8', errors='replace')`, and its docstring accepts this: binary content still counts by size via replacement. After the dependency and cache exclusion (basicly-jr0l.63) the remaining hazard is project-tracked binaries - most sharply `.beads/beads.db` plus its WAL and SHM, measured at 234 MB on this machine, which a scope of `**` or `.beads/**` will read fully into memory.

Deliberately left out of jr0l.63 to keep that diff to the stated defect. The fix is a size or binary guard rather than another directory name, because .beads is legitimate scope for a tracker-related bead.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `tests/test_decompose.py`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given a declared scope matching a binary or very large file when the working set is estimated then that file does not dominate the estimate
- Given a declared scope matching ordinary source files when the working set is estimated then the figure is unchanged from before the guard

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: A file matched by a declared scope that is binary or very large contributes a bounded amount to the working-set estimate, and the bound applies before the file is fully read into memory. An ordinary source file's estimate stays at today's already-capped figure, not at a pre-cap baseline the tree no longer has.

When the plan, architecture and catalog READMEs contradict the tree or contradict each other in tracker counts, test counts, command tables and skill lists, I want every count, table and roadmap row to read from one generated source or to match the tree, so I can trust the documentation instead of re-typing numbers that go stale on the next commit.

## Context

Documentation contradicted by the tree or by itself.

1. implementation-plan.md §2 contradicts itself: line 87 says 88 open / 3 deferred / 371 closed and 14 unlabelled beads; line 165 in the same section says 60 open / 6 deferred / 332 closed and four unlabelled. Actual: 81 open / 3 deferred / 448 closed. Line 107 says 1416 collected tests, line 86 says 1557; actual 2131. Line 107 says an 8-check verify full and that basicly.toml declares nine; actual 12 and 13. Line 107 says 57 test files; actual 69.

2. architecture.md:729 gives a measured always-on table from 2026-07-31 of 10775 / 7894 / 8026 characters; measured now 11017 / 8136 / 8268, so copilot headroom is 732 not 974 - and the 974 figure is quoted in the plan too. Consider generating this table rather than hand-maintaining it.

3. architecture.md §8 command tables are behind the CLI: the install row omits permissions-build, the loop row omits preflight supervise session decisions answer decide and watch, the worktree row omits merge merge-queue and bg-isolation, and the release signature omits --shipping.

4. `.basicly/core/skills/README.md` lists a skill-creator skill that does not exist (it became catalog-authoring) and has 24 entries against 33 skill.yaml sources. `.basicly/core/hooks/README.md` lists 4 of the 11 wired hooks, describes pre-commit.py as a fixed four checks when it runs the config-driven fast set, and cites an architecture §11.6 that does not exist.

5. README.md:198 pillar 01 has a shipped row the authoritative §15.2 table does not, and drops a not-planned row §15.3 lists - while §15 itself declares that where the three disagree the architecture wins and admits nothing gates it. CONTRIBUTING.md:79 states the commit rule without the minimum description length or the breaking-change marker the hook enforces.

- `.basicly/core/skills/README.md`

- Given the plan section 2 when it is read then it states one tracker count one test count and one verify-check count and each matches the tree
- Given the always-on character table when it is read then it matches a fresh measurement or is generated
- Given the architecture command tables when they are read then they list every subcommand the CLI ships
- Given the catalog READMEs when they are read then they name only skills and hooks that exist and resolve every cross reference
- Given the roadmap when it appears in more than one place then the copies agree with the authoritative table

Every tracker, test or check count a document states matches the tree or comes from a generated block. ## Trigger

When the rubric judge's metering is asserted only by a stubbed flag while the decider's metering is proven against real spend records, I want the same meter-level proof for the judge, so I can trust that every validated lane is actually metered rather than merely flagged as metered.

## Context

The four residual findings from the 2026-08-03 review of `basicly-gczc`, none blocking, grouped because they are all one theme: the judge half of that fix is asserted more weakly than the decider half, and three small claims are wider than what a test pins.

1. **The judge has no meter-level proof.** `tests/test_decisions.py` asserts `policy.spend_status(...).halted is False` over records the real `record_dispatch` wrote, plus a control that fails without the fix. The judge side asserts `seen['capture_usage'] is True` and stubs `record_dispatch` out entirely in its unwrap test. Per the rule the bead itself invoked - a passing parser is not evidence about a fail-open gate - the judge deserves the same assertion, and it matters more, because `rubrics.evaluate` runs on **every** validated lane while the decider runs only on a delegated decision.

2. **`basicly runner dry-run` prints an argv a real dispatch would not send.** `cli.py:3525` does not pass `capture_usage`, so the printed command omits the usage flags a metered dispatch appends. Harmless to metering, but `runner.py:226` claims every command is printable via `runner dry-run`, and this one is printable as something else.

3. **Two documented branches of the new code have no test.** `_claude_result_field`'s `isinstance(value, str)` guard is justified in prose by an `is_error` envelope carrying a structured payload under `result`, and no test passes a non-string `result` - the existing case only covers the key being absent. `_codex_agent_message`'s tolerance of a truncated final line is likewise asserted in prose only.

4. **Two tests key on a literal token appearing in a comment.** `tests/test_decisions.py` and `tests/test_rubrics.py` use `inspect.getsource` to require the string `capture_usage` in nearby prose. They do discriminate - both fail on revert - but a future reword to 'usage capture' fails them for no behavioural reason. Acceptable given the defect class they guard (a comment asserting a property the code lacked), so this is a recorded coupling rather than a defect: decide deliberately whether to keep it.

Reviewer coverage boundary, recorded so it is not assumed away: no agent CLI was invoked during that review, so the probe figures in `b512487`'s message were not independently reproduced, and the codex `item.completed`/`agent_message` shape rests on the earlier probe pinned in `tests/test_runner.py`.

## Scope

- `tests/test_rubrics.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_cli_runner.py`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: A test asserts spend status is not halted, over records the real dispatch recorder wrote for the rubric judge, with a control that fails without the metering flag. `runner dry-run` prints the argv a metered dispatch actually sends. The non-string result-field branch and the truncated-final-line branch each have a test.

## Trigger

When the path-restore form of `git checkout`, plus `git restore` and `git stash`, can discard uncommitted work with nothing refusing them, I want a mechanical deny rule for that family beside the other destructive-command backstops, so I can stop losing edits to a command the rules already name but do not block.

## The failure this comes from

I ran `git checkout HEAD -- tests/test_cli.py` during basicly-vkh0.42 and lost two of my
own uncommitted edits. Nothing refused it. The `require-explicit-confirmation` fragment
names the family in as many words, and the permissions comment
(`.basicly/core/permissions/permissions.yaml:34`) names these three commands *specifically*
as undenied — so the rule was written, read and still not followed.

**Root cause: the rule lives only in prose, and prose is advisory at the moment of the
call.** Every neighbouring family in that file has a mechanical backstop —
`destructive-rm`, `destructive-git`, `bypass-gates`, `force-push`. This one has a comment
explaining why it does not. The asymmetry is what made it the family that got through.

## The control

A `destructive-restore` deny entry beside `destructive-git`:

```yaml
  - id: destructive-restore
    description: block path-restore and stash, which discard uncommitted work silently
    claude:
      - "Bash(git checkout --*)"
      - "Bash(git checkout*--*)"
      - "Bash(git restore*)"
      - "Bash(git stash*)"
    copilot:
      - "shell(git restore)"
      - "shell(git stash)"
```

`git checkout <branch>` and `git checkout -b` stay allowed, which is what the loop's own
branch handling needs. The engine drives git through `subprocess`, not through the Bash
tool, so no deny rule reaches it — verify that before landing rather than assuming it.

Then rewrite the comment at lines 33-37: it currently teaches the reader that these three
are undenied, which will be false.

**Editing the permissions catalog is on the confirmation list.** This record is the
proposal; a human disposes of it.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/permissions/permissions.yaml`
- `.claude/settings.json`
- `tests/test_permissions.py`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given the projected `.claude/settings.json` when it is read then it carries a deny rule
  matching `git checkout -- <path>`, `git restore` and `git stash`
- Given `git checkout -b <name>` and `git checkout <branch>` when either is attempted then
  neither is denied, proven by a matcher probe rather than by inspection
- Given `permissions-check` when it runs then it passes with the new entry projected

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The projected `.claude/settings.json` carries a deny rule matching the path-restore form of `git checkout`, plus `git restore` and `git stash`. Checking out an existing branch by name, or creating one with `-b`, stays allowed, proven by a matcher probe rather than by inspection. `permissions-check` passes with the new entry projected, and the permissions comment no longer claims these commands are undenied.

## Trigger

When a scripted multi-line regex reports the right match count but deletes far more lines than intended, I want the `non-interactive-shell` fragment to require a line-delta check after a scripted in-place edit, so I can catch a wrong-sized match that a site count alone cannot see.

## The failure this comes from

A multi-line regex I ran over `tests/test_decompose.py` during basicly-vkh0.42 removed
**1644 lines**. The pattern was `(?:    .*
)+?(?=

)`, intended to cut one indented
block; the lazy quantifier still spanned every blank-line-separated run in the file. The
module was restored from HEAD and every edit reapplied by hand.

## Why the existing rule did not catch it

The `non-interactive-shell` fragment already says to name the expected site count before a
scripted multi-site replace and reconcile after. It did not bind here, for two reasons:

- **A deletion's site count was right.** One match, as predicted. The match was the wrong
  *size*, and a count of matches cannot see size.
- The rule reads as being about replacement, so an edit framed as a cut does not obviously
  fall under it.

## The control

Extend that fragment with the magnitude clause: after any scripted in-place edit, compare
`wc -l` before and against after, and name the expected delta first. A delta larger than
the change described is a stop, the same way a site-count delta is. One line, in the
fragment that already carries the site-count rule, so it lands in every agent's always-on
baseline — check the character budget before adding, since that baseline is at its cap.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/fragments/non-interactive-shell.yaml`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given the `non-interactive-shell` fragment when it is read then it names the line-delta
  reconciliation for a scripted in-place edit, distinct from the site-count rule
- Given the projected instruction files when `basicly check` runs then every per-target
  character cap still passes

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The `non-interactive-shell` fragment names a line-delta reconciliation step for a scripted in-place edit, distinct from the existing site-count rule. Every projected instruction file still passes its per-target character cap after the addition.

## Trigger

When the local toolchain and continuous integration resolve different versions of `uv`, node and git with nothing declaring an expected version, I want a declared version or range per tool checked on both sides, so I can stop a gate from passing or failing depending on which machine ran it.

## The defect

The repository declares one toolchain floor, `requires-python = ">=3.14"`, and pins nothing else. Continuous integration floats `uv` to latest and pins node to an older major than this machine runs, so a gate can pass locally and fail in continuous integration, or the reverse, and no measurement would say which.

Measured 2026-08-19.

| tool | this machine | continuous integration | direction of skew |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| uv | 0.11.28 | unpinned, `astral-sh/setup-uv@v7` resolves latest, which is 0.12.5 released 2026-08-14 | local **behind** |
| node | 24.18.0 | `node-version: 22` in two workflows | local **ahead** by two majors |
| git | 2.43.0, and the distribution candidate is also 2.43.0 | `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`, whatever that image ships | local behind, by an unmeasured amount |
| python | 3.14.6 | resolved by uv from `requires-python` | local behind 3.14.7, released 2026-08-05 |

## Why this is a defect rather than housekeeping

A behaviour difference between the two is already demonstrable. `uv init` gained a default build system in uv 0.12.0, released 2026-08-28... corrected: released 2026-07-28. So the same command produces a different project layout on this machine than in continuous integration, today. `uv init --help` on 0.11.28 lists both `--package` and `--no-package`, so a flag probe does not reveal it and only running the command does.

The repository is a distribution installed into other repositories, so its own gates are the product. A gate whose outcome depends on an unpinned tool version is a gate whose outcome nobody can reproduce.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `uv --version` locally and read 0.11.28.
2. Read `.github/workflows/quality-gates.yml` and `basicly.yml` and observe `astral-sh/setup-uv@v7` with no version input.
3. Fetch the current uv release and observe 0.12.5.
4. Read `node-version: 22` in both workflows and compare with `node --version` locally, 24.18.0.
5. Observe that no file in the tree states a version for uv, node or git.

Observed: three tools skew in two directions and nothing declares an expected version.
Expected: the toolchain a gate runs on is declared, and a difference is visible rather than latent.

## The decision this needs, recorded rather than assumed

Whether to pin continuous integration to the local toolchain, or to raise the local toolchain to what continuous integration resolves, or to declare a floor and a ceiling per tool and check both. This record does not choose. What it refuses is the current state, where neither side is declared.

## Scope

- `.github/workflows/`
- `pyproject.toml`
- `.scripts/`
- `tests/`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: A declared version or range answers, per tool, what continuous integration and a local run expect for `uv`, node and git. Continuous integration provisions the declared version instead of resolving latest. A local toolchain outside the declared range is reported rather than passing silently, and a new tool release does not fail anything until a human widens the range.

## Trigger

When a landing scope check treats a regenerated path as foreign, and one scope collision holds every other built lane for the whole pass, I want the check to exclude regenerated paths and the supervisor to stop holding unrelated lanes on a scope-only failure, so I can land the other lanes without paying rework for a regenerated block.

## Context

2026-08-28, truth epic: basicly-0cpn51's landing was routed to rework because it changed `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` outside its scope, and basicly-tjhjmk declared that path. The change is the `plan-current-state` generated block re-counting test files, which the landing's own regeneration produces for every lane that adds a test module; `[worktree.regenerate_commands]` already names the path as generated so a conflict there is rebuilt without rework. The scope gate does not read that table, so the same path is generated for the merge and foreign for the scope check. basicly-3oxf0d, basicly-tjhjmk and basicly-0cpn51 each paid a rework and a hand-widened scope for it; basicly-e2mz.18 records the sibling shape for the harness's own per-lane files.

Second half, same round: the supervisor holds every other lane "after an earlier failure this pass" when the first failure is a scope collision, and with no lane to dispatch it repeats the identical pass until `--max-passes` (basicly-n5jvhh's shape). Four built lanes sat unlanded behind one scope finding for three passes.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge_scope.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_merge_scope.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.fixed.md`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: a landing that regenerates `plan-current-state` passes the scope gate with the path reported as regenerated, and a pass with one scope failure lands its other lanes.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: A path named in `[worktree.regenerate_commands]` is excluded from the scope comparison and reported as regenerated rather than as a scope violation. A lane's scope-collision failure does not hold the other lanes of the pass. A pass that dispatches no lane and repeats the previous pass's routed outcome stops and routes to a human instead of running again.
